storylines.label: DeepSeek Open-sources
storylines.latest_title: Supercharging XLA-Based Inference: Announcing the Launch of XLA Serving Engine

editorial.tldr: DeepSeek tied its V4.1-Flash model to its own agent harness on Oct 17, then on Oct 20 open-sourced DeepInfer, the inference engine behind its production services. On Oct 31 it published the architecture of an always-on coding agent, dsh-superagent.
editorial.whats_new: Coverage of the dsh-superagent prototype, a router-worker coding agent that watches team chat for work, continued through Nov 4, while the rest of the thread is third-party inference-engine news.
editorial.why_it_matters: DeepSeek is releasing both the serving layer (DeepInfer, reportedly 155T tokens/day) and an agent harness, so platform teams can inspect a production-scale stack, but the cost and throughput figures come from DeepSeek and press reports, not independent benchmarks.
editorial.take_for_builders: Before adopting DeepInfer or dsh-superagent, check license terms and hardware support, and benchmark them against your current serving stack rather than relying on the quoted token-per-day numbers.

status.detail: Two DeepSeek open-source drops, DeepInfer and dsh-superagent, with no independent benchmarks yet.

storylines.label: Kimi K3.1
storylines.latest_title: Zero Mismatch, Simple Async RL: REINFORCE Zero, DeepSeek-V4.1 and Kimi K3.1

editorial.tldr: Kimi K3.1 surfaced as an unreleased name after Arena testing, then Moonshot launched the roughly 3T-parameter K3.1 Pro on Oct 24. A quota-driven rocky rollout was followed by third-party hosting, vLLM day-0 support and, on Nov 5, full open weights.
editorial.whats_new: vLLM's Nov 6 post uses Kimi K3.1 as a test case for zero-mismatch async RL, aligning rollout and training kernels bit for bit one day after the full weights shipped.
editorial.why_it_matters: K3.1 Pro is now self-hostable on vLLM and Ascend, and vLLM's RL work shows it is also a fine-tuning target. Licence terms and a 1.56TB footprint decide whether that beats third-party hosts or first-party quotas.
editorial.take_for_builders: Read the weights licence conditions before planning a self-host, and budget for 1.56TB of storage. Pin the vLLM version and rerun your own evals against Opus 5.5 before changing routing; for RL, check the bit-for-bit kernel alignment in vLLM's post first.

status.detail: K3.1 Pro moved from a quota-troubled first-party launch to third-party hosting, vLLM support and a full weights release; vLLM now documents RL training with it. Independent quality and cost data are still thin.

storylines.label: Large Language
storylines.latest_title: Show HN: Thinker – Trim context and cache knowledge to extend agent usage limits

editorial.tldr: This thread is a broad reading list on LLM behavior, reliability and knowledge. Oct 16-28 papers covered sycophancy, hallucination, steering and evals, then Mistral Large 4 landed on Hugging Face and vLLM on Oct 29 as work shifted to memory and retrieval.
editorial.whats_new: Nov 2-5: Anthropic reported zkSNARK progress for provable inference, and a Show HN tool, Thinker, trims context and caches knowledge to stretch agent token limits.
editorial.why_it_matters: The practical thread is context cost and knowledge handling: retrieval, memory and context trimming decide agent reliability and token spend more than any single model release here.
editorial.take_for_builders: If agent token limits bite, measure context trimming and caching against your own eval set before adopting it; treat the preprints and the Show HN tool as unreplicated.

storylines.label: Attention Context
storylines.latest_title: Muir: Linear Attention with Sensitivity-Allocated Gating and Matched-Filter Readout

editorial.tldr: Late-October papers attacked long-context cost from several sides: isolating context in chain of thought, initializing linear-attention memory, and learned sparse attention. By early November the work moved to production sparse attention, TPU kernels and agent-side context compression.
editorial.whats_new: Muir (Nov 5) reworks gated delta-rule linear attention with sensitivity-allocated gating, while QRAE compresses DeepSearch agent context using query-relevant attention entropy.
editorial.why_it_matters: Long-context cost drives inference spend and latency for agents. Sparse and linear attention variants, plus agent-level context compression, are the levers that decide how much context a deployment can afford.
editorial.take_for_builders: These are preprints with no shared benchmark, so do not plan around them yet. Track which ones ship in open-weight models or serving stacks, and rerun your long-context retrieval evals before adopting any.

storylines.label: Diffusion Language
storylines.latest_title: SpecCTMC: Exact Speculative Simulation of Diffusion Language Model Continuous-Time Markov Chains

editorial.tldr: Diffusion language models first surfaced here on the offensive side, as a way to craft fluent low-perplexity black-box attacks on LLMs. Two decoding-speed papers followed, cutting rounds via schedule distillation and adaptive compute for agents.
editorial.whats_new: SpecCTMC proposes exact speculative simulation of masked diffusion LMs, keeping the output distribution intact while sampling multiple tokens in parallel; it follows length-extrapolation and multimodal hallucination papers.
editorial.why_it_matters: Diffusion LLMs only pay off for serving if parallel decoding cuts rounds without changing output quality; SpecCTMC targets exactly that, but it is still research-stage evidence, not a deployable runtime.
editorial.take_for_builders: Do not plan serving capacity around diffusion LLMs yet; if you prototype one, measure decoding rounds, output-distribution drift and quality against your autoregressive baseline, and include fluent-prompt attacks in red-team evals.

status.detail: Six arXiv papers, no production release: attacks, decoding speed, length extrapolation and multimodal reliability.

storylines.label: Environment Synthesis
storylines.latest_title: Agent-R$^2$: Scaling Agents for Realistic Productivity Work via Real-Source Data Synthesis

editorial.tldr: In October, papers began synthesizing training environments for agents instead of collecting human demonstrations, first for computer use and then for tool use with controllable data composition. By November the work moved to MCP tool-centric synthesis and to real-source data for productivity tasks.
editorial.whats_new: Agent-R² (Nov 5) synthesizes training data from real sources to target realistic productivity work, the fourth environment-synthesis paper in 17 days.
editorial.why_it_matters: If agent capability now scales with synthesized environments, tool and MCP coverage in training data decides how well agents handle your own tool surface, and evals built on public environments may overlap with training data.
editorial.take_for_builders: Treat these as preprints: before adopting any synthesized-environment model, rerun it on your own MCP tools and check whether its benchmark environments overlap with your eval set.

status.detail: Four arXiv papers in three weeks converge on synthesized environments as the way to scale agent training; none is independently replicated yet.

storylines.label: Reasoning Execution
storylines.latest_title: MCPHallu: Benchmarking Reasoning, Execution, and Memory Hallucinations in MCP Agents

editorial.tldr: Two October papers treated the gap between an agent's reasoning and its tool execution as a design surface: speculative execution to cut voice-agent latency, and a Petri-net supervisor to block unsafe calls. A November benchmark then measured where MCP agents fail across that gap.
editorial.whats_new: MCPHallu (Nov 5) benchmarks reasoning, execution, and memory hallucinations in MCP agents, shifting the thread from proposed harnesses to measured failure modes.
editorial.why_it_matters: Agents calling tools across multiple MCP servers fail in distinct ways: wrong plans, wrong calls, wrong recall. Latency tricks and safety gates between reasoning and action both change where those failures surface.
editorial.take_for_builders: Log reasoning, tool-call, and memory errors separately in your MCP agent evals, and treat the papers' harness and speculation results as unreplicated until you test them on your own tools.

status.detail: Research papers only so far; no production implementation or independent replication in this thread.

storylines.label: Prompt Injection
storylines.latest_title: Beyond Instruction Override: Benchmarking Indirect Prompt Injection with Task-Tampering Attacks

editorial.tldr: Late October papers proposed model-level defenses: learned attention gates (Heads of Security) and adversarial training (SecPO). Early November papers then widened the attack surface to persistent agent memory and silently updated tools.
editorial.whats_new: A new benchmark shows indirect prompt injection can tamper with a tool-using agent's task outcome rather than just redirect it, a case most IPI benchmarks do not test.
editorial.why_it_matters: Defenses tuned to block instruction override can miss attacks that corrupt memory, tool updates, or task results; test those paths before trusting a guardrail.
editorial.take_for_builders: Add a task-tampering case, a cross-session memory-poisoning case, and a tool-version-change check to your agent red-team suite, and do not rely on instruction-override tests alone.

status.detail: Research is shifting from single-turn instruction override to memory, tool-update, and task-tampering attacks, with new runtime defenses alongside.

storylines.label: Policy Optimization
storylines.latest_title: Learning Multi-Agent Orchestration:Higher-Order Interactions in Policy Improvement

editorial.tldr: ReflectPO (Oct 22) and SOPO (Oct 23) applied policy optimization to long-horizon agents and span-level hallucination detection. By Oct 27-28 papers argued the policy and its harness must be judged together, and Snyk VulnBench 2.0 measured harness policy and cost against deterministic SAST.
editorial.whats_new: A Nov 5 preprint on learned multi-agent orchestration models higher-order interactions in policy improvement, following Nov 4's PromptOps for LLM-as-a-judge drift and tree-branching TSBPO (Oct 30).
editorial.why_it_matters: Optimization targets are widening from the model to the orchestrator, the prompt and the judge, so each moving part of an agent stack needs its own regression eval.
editorial.take_for_builders: Treat these as preprints: wait for code and replication before changing a training pipeline, and rerun agent evals whenever the harness, prompt or judge changes, not only the model.

status.detail: Preprint-only thread: methods span agents, judges and orchestration, with no code or replication reported in these items.

storylines.label: Reasoning Latent
storylines.latest_title: [AINews] Behind Latent Space: Kill My SaaS, Jev & AI in 2026 | AIEi Shanghai

editorial.tldr: An Oct 18 paper proposed hybrid agents that reason in latent space but act through text. A paper on Oct 27 then applied latent reasoning to multi-agent systems by storing reusable skills in compact external memory.
editorial.whats_new: No new latent-reasoning research landed after Oct 30; the Nov 4 item is a Latent Space newsletter that matched on name only, so the thread is still three unreplicated preprints.
editorial.why_it_matters: Latent reasoning aims to cut inference cost by keeping intermediate steps out of text, but it also makes those steps harder to inspect and log.
editorial.take_for_builders: These are unreplicated preprints; if you log reasoning traces for debugging, check what your tooling would lose before adopting latent-reasoning models.

storylines.label: Routing Learning
storylines.latest_title: Visual Token Routing: Learning to keep tokens that matter

editorial.tldr: Three unrelated arXiv papers share the word routing: expert routing for respiratory-sound classifiers under device drift (Oct 20), then strategy-guided RL for picking agent skills (Oct 30). The link is vocabulary, not a continuing research line.
editorial.whats_new: A Nov 4 arXiv paper learns which visual tokens a computer-use agent keeps, targeting the compute cost of long-horizon and real-time agent tasks.
editorial.why_it_matters: Learned routing is showing up in agent cost control (skills, tokens), but these are single-paper claims with no shared benchmark or released tooling.
editorial.take_for_builders: Treat these as ideas to watch: if you run computer-use agents, wait for reproducible cost numbers before changing token or skill selection.

status.detail: Three papers from two arXiv feeds reuse the routing idea in different domains; no cross-citation or common evaluation is shown.

storylines.label: Image Editing
storylines.latest_title: TailSteer: Trajectory-Tail Steering for Drift-Resistant Multi-turn Image Editing

editorial.tldr: Papers began treating image editing as a serving problem: EditJev routed each request across editing models because per-sample quality varies widely. MoI-Bench then benchmarked on-device editing, and RetryRoute added cost-aware routing for critique-and-retry loops.
editorial.whats_new: TailSteer (Nov 4) targets multi-turn editing, where small unintended changes accumulate into visual drift even when single-turn quality is strong.
editorial.why_it_matters: Editing models differ in cost by over an order of magnitude and in per-sample quality, so routing, retry policy and multi-turn drift become reliability and cost levers for any service that edits images.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you run an edit-and-retry loop, log per-model reject rates and cost per accepted edit now, and cap multi-turn chains or re-anchor to the original image until drift fixes are independently verified.
